answers.body:
**Question:** Create a Dockerfile to deploy an Apache HTTP Server which hosts a custom main page

**Solution:**

Create a `Dockerfile` that extends the official Apache `httpd` image and writes a custom `index.html`:

```Dockerfile
FROM docker.io/httpd:2.4
RUN echo "Hello, World!" > /usr/local/apache2/htdocs/index.html
```

Alternatively you can use `FROM httpd:2.4` (the `docker.io/` prefix is implicit).

---

**Question:** Build and see how many layers the image consists of

**Solution:**

Build the image with tag `simpleapp`:

```bash
podman build -t simpleapp .
```

List built images:

```bash
podman images
```

Show the image layer tree:

```bash
podman image tree localhost/simpleapp:latest
```

---

checks.label: Built the image with podman build

answers.body:
**Question:** Run the image locally, inspect its status and logs, finally test that it responds as expected

**Solution:**

Run the image in detached mode with port mapping 8080→80:

```bash
podman run -d --name test -p 8080:80 localhost/simpleapp
```

Inspect status:

```bash
podman ps
```

Check the logs:

```bash
podman logs test
```

Test the response:

```bash
curl 0.0.0.0:8080
```

---

**Question:** Run a command inside the pod to print out the index.html file

**Solution:**

```bash
podman exec test cat /usr/local/apache2/htdocs/index.html
```

---

checks.label: Ran a command inside the container (exec)

answers.body:
**Question:** Tag the image with ip and port of a private local registry and then push the image to this registry

**Solution:**

> Note: Some small Kubernetes distributions (such as [microk8s](https://microk8s.io/docs/registry-built-in)) have a built-in registry you can use for this exercise. If this is not your case, you'll have to set up one on your own.

Tag the image with the registry's address, then push it:

```bash
podman tag localhost/simpleapp $REGISTRY_IP:5000/simpleapp
podman push $REGISTRY_IP:5000/simpleapp
```

---

checks.label: Tagged the image for the registry
Pushed the image to the registry

answers.body:
**Question:** Create a container without running/starting it

**Solution:**

Use `podman create` to create a container without starting it:

```bash
podman create busybox
```

Verify it exists (in `Created` state):

```bash
podman container ls -a
```

---

checks.label: Created a container without starting it

answers.body:
**Question:** Export a container to output.tar file

**Solution:**

List containers to find the one you just created, then export it.

```bash
podman container ls -a
podman export <container-id> --output=output.tar
ls -al output.tar
```

Replace `<container-id>` with the actual id from `podman container ls -a`.

---

checks.label: Exported the container to a tar file

answers.body:
**Question:** Run a pod with the image pushed to the registry

**Solution:**

Use kubectl to run the image you pushed to the registry:

```bash
kubectl run simpleapp --image=$REGISTRY_IP:5000/simpleapp --port=80
```

Verify and curl the application:

```bash
kubectl get pod simpleapp -o wide
kubectl exec simpleapp -- curl -s localhost
```

---

checks.label: Ran a pod from the pushed image

answers.body:
**Question:** Log into a remote registry server and then read the credentials from the default file

**Solution:**

> Note: Two common free registry servers for this exercise are [DockerHub](https://hub.docker.com/) and [Quay.io](https://quay.io/).

Log in to the registry:

```bash
podman login --username $YOUR_USER --password $YOUR_PWD docker.io
```

Read the credentials file (location depends on `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`):

```bash
cat ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/containers/auth.json
```

For rootless Podman, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is typically `/run/user/$(id -u)`.

---

**Question:** Create a secret both from existing login credentials and from the CLI

**Solution:**

Create a secret from the auth.json file written by `podman login` (note: `kubernetes.io/dockercfgjson` is the type for `~/.dockercfg` legacy format; for `auth.json` use `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` even though the file shape differs — Kubernetes only needs the auths blob):

```bash
kubectl create secret generic mysecret \
  --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}/containers/auth.json \
  --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
```

Create a docker-registry secret from the CLI (preferred form, properly typed):

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry mysecret2 \
  --docker-server=https://index.docker.io/v1/ \
  --docker-username=$YOUR_USER \
  --docker-password=$YOUR_PWD
```

---

**Question:** Create the manifest for a Pod that uses one of the two secrets just created to pull an image hosted on the relative private remote registry

**Solution:**

Save the following as `private-reg-pod.yaml` (replace `$YOUR_PRIVATE_IMAGE` with the real image path), then apply it.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: private-reg
spec:
  containers:
  - name: private-reg-container
    image: $YOUR_PRIVATE_IMAGE
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: mysecret
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f private-reg-pod.yaml
```

---

**Question:** Clean up all the images and containers

**Solution:**

Remove all containers (force, including running ones) and all images from the local Podman storage, then delete the pod you created for the registry:

```bash
podman rm --all --force
podman rmi --all
kubectl delete pod simpleapp
```

---

checks.label: Cleaned up containers with podman rm
